analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that block workers from taking new jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban most noncompete agreements never got a vote; it sat in two House committees from February 2023 until the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to use noncompete agreements — contract clauses that stop workers from leaving for a competing employer — except in narrow cases like someone selling a business. Employers could still protect trade secrets and use nondisclosure agreements. The Federal Trade Commission and Labor Department would enforce the ban, and workers could sue in court. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one in five American workers economists estimate are covered by noncompete agreements, across sectors and income brackets. Banning them would let workers change jobs freely, which the bill's findings say would raise wages, speed innovation, and boost productivity. Workers could also sue employers who try to enforce noncompetes, with attorney's fees available, and could not be forced into arbitration or barred from class actions over violations.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits entering into, enforcing, or attempting to enforce noncompete agreements with employees and contractors, voiding such agreements going forward [S3]
Allows workers to sue in federal court for actual damages plus attorney's fees, and blocks forced arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims [S3]
Gives the FTC and Labor Department enforcement power, requires employers to post notice of the ban, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on noncompetes to hold onto trained workers would lose that tool and would face enforcement by the FTC, the Labor Department, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits. They would still be able to use trade secret law, intellectual property protections, and nondisclosure agreements.

drawbacks.text: Employers could still impose one-year noncompetes on senior executives as part of a sale with severance, a carve-out that keeps the restriction for the highest-paid officials [S3]
A blanket federal ban would override the state-by-state approach most states take, which typically allow noncompetes only when narrow, reasonable, and sometimes only above a wage threshold [S3]

A good-faith objection is that employers lose a contractual way to protect investments in training and confidential customer relationships, though the bill preserves trade secret and nondisclosure remedies [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most workers the benefits are direct and the costs indirect: freedom to change jobs, more bargaining power, and likely wage gains, while employers retain trade secret and nondisclosure tools for their most legitimate concerns. The main trade-offs are the loss of a cheap retention tool for employers and the senior-executive carve-out, which is modest. The design is broadly workable; the bill's failure was about never getting consideration, not about a defeated compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee in its first week, and no committee ever voted on it before the congressional term ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 1, 2023 by Rep. Scott Peters with Reps. Gallagher (R) and Eshoo (D) as original cosponsors [S3]
Referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee [S1]
On February 10, 2023 referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after that [S5]
The bill had only three cosponsors total (two Republicans, one Democrat) at the end of the Congress [S4]
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and any bill not passed dies with it [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use noncompete agreements to limit where their workers can go next are better off, since no ban took effect. The roughly one in five workers covered by noncompetes gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat sponsor with two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors [S4] — but with only three cosponsors the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would strip them of a contract tool that economists estimate covers one in five workers, forcing them to rely on trade secret and nondisclosure protections instead. Their gain from blocking it comes at the cost of workers' job mobility and wages [S3].

industries.industry: Business sellers, senior executives, and professional partnerships
industries.note: The bill preserves noncompetes for people selling a business and for top executives with severance agreements, keeping those restrictions lawful even as it bans the rest [S3].
